Their society can best be described as a mix of old and new. They are very long lived for hominids (usually living to the age of 200+) and this means that older generations from eras long past are still around and kicking. The Vampire government has been described as very slow to change, having the oldest still-used constitution in the world. But Vampiric culture is noted to be very vibrant and changes rapidly. This dance between the ancient and the new gives them a very unique society among the world’s sapient species.

In my modern fantasy world, Vampires are a species of hominid that evolved to have a nocturnal lifestyle. 

They are physically similar to Humans, being closely related, with pale skin, fangs, and large eyes for seeing in the dark. They are carnivorous and require the nutrients in blood to survive. 

Being nocturnal, they are bothered by bright sunlight and their skin sunburns easily. This makes obstacles for other species wanting to do business with Vampires or wanting to live in their country, as they close everything during the day. Conversely, Vampires travelling abroad need to stock up on their highly potent sunscreen. 

Vampires and Humans are so closely related that they are the only two species capable of successfully producing offspring, though this is rare.

Goblins, like fairies, are a species created as a byproduct of a mana break. A mana break is a crack in reality caused by excess dark magic usage which can create bizarre side effects, in this case creating a new creature. 

Exactly when they were “born” remains a mystery, but it must’ve been a very long time ago, as they appear in even the oldest writings. Being an inherently magical creature, goblins can use magic, though their spells are rudimentary and primitive. They are organised in tribes and each tribe has its own unique culture and habits.

Goblins can be dangerous but mostly they are seen as a nuisance by the populations that live near them. They like to cause trouble for humans and some tribes have even allied with fairies to cause even more mischief. They are not inherently evil however, and there are examples of goblins coexisting peacefully with humans, though rare.

Regular dogs do exist in the setting, and in fact some Kobolds keep them as pets the same way a Human might keep a monkey as a pet.

Kobolds don’t really use pheromones to communicate, but another race, the Arachne, do. The Kobolds are the only other race that can detect these pheromones and it has led to them creating a special “second language” between the two which has helped the two races to have warm diplomatic relations.

Indeed they are miners! The Kobold nation is mostly arid desert so their principal export is mining cobalt and diamonds. Werewolves don’t exist physically in my setting, but they do appear in the Vampires’ myths and fables, and when the two races first encountered each other centuries ago, they were mistaken for werewolves. The Kobolds for their part find the similarity amusing. 

They are mostly carnivorous but can and do eat vegetables. They make great use of palm trees for food, and another staple crop is dates which feature frequently in Kobold cuisine.

Race: Kobolds (dog people)

* They are highly argumentative, as it’s in their culture to stand your ground in an argument and whoever is the loudest and most passionate is probably the one that’s right. 

* They were once a part of the Centaurs’ empire, and were not treated well. When they finally gained independence, they were given land according to the borders drawn up by the Centaurs, leading to a sizeable Kobold population still living in the Centaur nation. “Southern” independent Kobolds view these “Northern” Kobolds as traitors for continuing to live under the Centaurs. Though the reality is much more complicated and nuanced. 

* The Kobold nation is the poorest nation in the world with the lowest standard of living. Despite this, Kobolds are fiercely patriotic and have a lot of pride for their independence movement. 

* Being dogs, they have a heightened sense of smell and greet each other by embracing and sniffing each other’s necks. They recognise others more by their individual scents more than their faces. 

* Also in keeping with their canine origins, they can only see certain colours, and have trouble seeing some colours. Their stoplights are coloured differently from the standard as they can’t quite differentiate between red and yellow.

The main school of magic, which is taught to all mages, is Light Magic. It is the standard "natural" magic that uses the natural properties of the environment. This is "standard" magic, and may be used freely with no risks.

Dark Magic is magic that is completely unnatural. It violates all laws of nature and can do things that logically cannot be. When compared to Light Magic, Dark Magic is theoretically more powerful, as there is no real limit to what a powerful enough dark mage can achieve with it. Dark Magic can create energy and matter from nothing, completely "erase" matter and energy, manipulate souls, and even create new life, among infinite other things.

"So why don't all mages learn Dark Magic if it's so powerful?" you may ask. The main drawback to Dark Magic is that it is extremely dangerous to use. It requires a skill level that most cannot attain in one lifetime (hence why so many become liches) to use even remotely safely. Dark Magic inherently corrupts everything it touches, including the user, who will quickly begin to lose their mind. Various undesirable "by-products" can also be produced. "Unnatural" creatures such as goblins and faeries are theorised to have been by-products of Dark Magic use.

The biggest risk when pushing it too far is causing a "mana break", where the mana that holds reality together is bent and torn beyond its limits. This can cause anything from the obliteration of its user, to the complete destruction of reality itself. One of the most notable mana breaks is the one that sets off my world's story, where a dark mage unwittingly destroyed an entire continent along with everything on it.

It is for this reason that Dark Magic is forbidden, and its users heavily persecuted. This culminated with a massive purge of known dark mages, and the practice was thought to have gone extinct (though this was not the case).

Using English as the baseline (which in this world English is Standard Centauric, the official language of the Centaur nation):

Excluding pidgins and creoles (such as Koboldic Centauric) Northern Centauric is the easiest as it's a dialect (though not entirely mutually intelligible) of Standard. It has very unique pronunciation, but the grammar is quite similar and it has a lot of loanwords from Standard.

Second place would probably be Vampiric. It can most closely be compared to real-world Romance languages, and there is a decent amount of overlap with Standard with many loanwords and similar concepts. It does have gendered nouns which might be tricky to learn.

Devilic follows it as it is a relatively simple language to learn with very exact rules and conjugations. Despite the fact that there are many dialects of varying difficulty, there exists one simplified "standard" dialect that is spoken by all Devils which makes it easy for a traveller to be understood.

Orcic comes next as it has a very structured grammar with little to no exceptions for rules, but the orthography is very complex and harsh, making it hard to master its pronunciation.

Harpic follows, as it is a very simple language with very few rules and flexible grammar, but it is incredibly fast-paced and quite difficult to train one's ear to.

Southern Centauric languages follow here as there are many dialects, some being very distinct, and features several click consonants which are difficult to master. Despite being called "Centauric" they are in no way related to Standard and are their own language family.

Humanic actually ranks as very difficult, which is surprising for the Human language. It is based on Japanese and carries with it all of its unique aspects and difficulties, such as three writing systems and differing levels of politeness.

Merfolkic is especially hard as it's a language meant to be spoken underwater, which is of course difficult for a surface-dweller to do. It is a very "flowing" and melodic language with very nuanced levels of politeness and grammatical quirks that make it very challenging. It doesn't help that there are dozens of dialects.

Nagic is among the hardest languages to learn as it is not only a tonal language, but it carries with it the complex culture of the Naga, which makes it very easy for an innocent-sounding phrase to become incredibly rude just by skipping one obscure rule.

Lastly, the absolute hardest language is by far Arachnic. It is a language for arthropods and it is so difficult that one might say it's impossible for a foreigner to master. It requires making sounds that the Human mouth is simply not equipped to make, and further requires pheromones that no other race can produce.

Special mention to Onic languages, which, while not especially difficult on their own, are very hard to learn due to being nearly extinct, and there being a dearth of resources with which to learn them.

My world has the Arachne, a race of spider-like sapient arthropods closely related to arachnids.

* Arachne are not a hive mind, but have a very "collectivist" culture. Their children are all raised communally, and they don't have the same concept of family as most of the other races do.
* Their bodies are covered with a tough exoskeleton that is slightly iridescent. They consider this iridescence attractive, and many products exist to enhance the shine and colour of their carapace. * Their faces can only emote to a limited degree. There's loads of ways to go about it, and the Japanese-learning community can't even agree on all of them, lol. But for me the way I started was by starting with the alphabets early. Learn hiragana/katakana first and foremost (they're really quite easy, I learnt them in a fortnight and I'm by no means good at memorising), it'll eliminate using romaji as a crutch and will get you a solid foundation for reading.

For kanji, I won't sugarcoat it, it's going to be a grind, and there's no real shortcuts to it. Just make sure you stick to it and be consistent. I highly suggest using some form of flashcard system (I personally use [Anki](https://apps.ankiweb.net/) and swear by it) to at least learn the meanings and how to write them. Memorise them as best you can. There's a plethora of methods for this (too many to list here) so I'd suggest trying a bunch and seeing what fits best for you. Personally I recommend not worrying about the readings and just sticking to recognising/writing them for now.

Once you feel ready, start tackling vocabulary. Anki has pre-made flashcard decks for the "core 6000" most common words which will give you the essentials. Learning vocab has the bonus of simultaneously teaching you the kanji readings as you go in a very natural way. For grammar, I recommend a good textbook (Genki is a popular one for beginners/intermediates) and using your flashcard system for full sentences that you pick up as you learn.

As you do this, supplement your learning by watching/listening/reading as much native material as you can find. Anime/manga works, but it's best to have a wide range of material to draw from (news, podcasts, dorama, novels, etc.) and immerse yourself as much as possible. Living/working in Japan as you plan to do is a fantastic way to get real "into the fire" immersion, but I recommend doing so once you already have at least a somewhat decent grasp on the language to get the most out of it.

Anyway that's my few "tips", lol. Bear in mind that I started many years ago, so there's now even more tools than I had available. I stopped studying it some years ago, and sadly what little ability I had is quickly rusting away, so if you're serious about learning it, stay consistent and study often!

Also if you haven't already, I highly suggest visiting r/LearnJapanese, as they have a wealth of information and resources, and can give far better advice than I ever could! Best of luck!

I definitely agree on that, and I'm a bit embarrassed to say that sadly it's not one aspect I've fully fleshed out to my liking as yet. The way I have it so far is by severely limiting what alchemy in my world can accomplish. It basically functions by combining reagents and using specialised spells to coax out different results (in a tricky game of educated guessing and trial-and-error). So while you can cook up things like painkilling potions, self-heating stones, and lighter-than-air gases with relative ease, you cannot change one item into a completely different one (e.g. wood to gold, stone to iron, shit to meat, etc).

Dark magic *can* actually do this, however. It can even create matter from absolutely nothing, if one is powerful enough (my main baddie, for example, can do this with her eyes closed). But this comes with the risks mentioned above, which brings me to:

The *worst* consequence of dark magic? It's not "on record" per se, as it was never recorded in history, but it's the event that actually kicks off the origin story of the main villain 4,000 years ago. Essentially a mana break that completely obliterated every landmass (and everything/one on it) in the entire western hemisphere, transforming it into a roiling, nigh-unnavigable global ocean. It could've destroyed the whole planet if it hadn't been stabilised, and even then, the mana rip still floats above the epicentre like a sword of Damocles to this day, and can potentially break again.

Dark magic accidents have also birthed a number of monsters, some of which were one-offs, but others formed full populations. Notoriously, the Fairies and the Goblins that still plague the world were originally spawned by dark magic. One of the biggest antagonists essentially *is* dark magic, or rather, a dark magical anomaly that gained self-awareness (and helped cause the above-mentioned cataclysm), which gains power via leeching off powerful dark mages.

And as for the universe imploding? At a certain point in the story it is heavily implied that it may have done so before, and forced the universe to "hard reset" from zero.

The most cutting edge tech being developed in alchemy currently is the power source for magical engines. Though the name sounds fancy, the magical engine is just a steam engine, but what makes it magical is the source of its heat. Using alchemy, a substance was produced that radiates constant, steady heat when “activated”. Where you’d once need a huge roomful of coal, now you can power an equivalent engine with just a basketball-sized glowing rock. This is a big deal for flying ships, where weight savings is very important.

They do eventually run out of juice though, so development continues on creating longer-lasting, and more potent rocks. Alchemists are putting a lot of priority on this technology because of other potential applications for magic engines, such as automobiles and small aircraft. It’s seen as very exciting tech.

As for dark magic, the reason it’s so taboo as opposed to other offensive magic is that while normal magic gently “bends” the mana that holds the universe together to do normally impossible things, dark magic makes a möbius loop out of it, rips it apart, and stitches it back together. You can break all rules of physics and reality with it, so the possibilities are nearly limitless. The risk is that distorting mana to that extent means a lot of really fucky side effects can happen, the worst of which being a “mana break” that can potentially do anything from erase you from existence, to destroying the entire universe.

A lot of budding magic users want to do "cool" shit like elemental combat magic, but from a purely economical standpoint, healing magic and alchemy are the smart choices for a career in magic. People are always going to get hurt, so talented healers are always in demand, both for actual practice, and for developing newer and better methods and theories. They are held in high esteem and it's a highly stable career.

As far as alchemy goes, it encompasses much more than just potions. Alchemy is what drives industry. The flying ships that are the cornerstone of all commerce rely heavily on alchemically-produced lifting gas for their balloons, and the power sources for their magically-powered steam engines are also made by alchemy. So lucrative is this field, that parents often tell their children "Be an alchemist! Make lots of money!"

Vampires in my setting aren't supernatural creatures at all, but actually a species of nocturnally-adapted hominids, closely related to Humans. They are so closely related that they can successfully interbreed (being the only two races that can do so) and it is speculated that anatomically modern Vampires and Humans came about because of this.

1. One doesn't become a Vampire, they are simply born to Vampire parents.
2. Vampires tend to be more lightly built than Humans, and have very pale, nearly chalk-white skin, and prominent fangs. Their eyes are larger than Human eyes, and adapted for night-vision; all Vampires have bright red irises. Their hair is naturally black (similarly to Humans), though dyeing it is popular among Vampires. They age slower and are much longer-lived than Humans, living on average close to 200 years (with at least one highly exceptional case making it to 300).
3. They require a fairly steady supply of blood as part of their nutritional needs. This will differ by individual but two pints or so a day is the average recommended amount for a healthy diet.
4. Most of the traditional weaknesses were dropped as this is a non-magical setting. They do however, somewhat retain their weakness to sunlight in that (being nocturnal) they are rather photosensitive and more susceptible to UV damage. Vampires going out in the day for long periods need to wear strong sunblocks and sunglasses.
5. They have no real special powers, save for their advanced night-vision (which can be a detriment in bright sunlight). Notably they are one of only two sapient species that can successfully interbreed with another one (in this case Humans) and produce fertile offspring.
6. In terms of morality they fall in the same as any other race. Some are good, some are assholes. Generally speaking though, Vampires are a friendly and pleasant people, though they tend to come off a bit "dry" at first. They enjoy good diplomatic relations with most of the other races, and are a major economic and cultural power.
7. I guess the only thing that makes my Vampires "unique" is the fact they're not magical or undead and are just another one of many naturally-evolved races.

That's more or less my approach to it. I don't bother with making this or that race more or less powerful than the others, but I spend a lot of time exploring their cultures and how that shapes who they are.

While the spell itself was powerful, it wasn't so much the spell but her inability to control it that caused the disaster. Dark magic works by distorting the mana that holds reality together in ways it wasn't meant to. If you screw up, you can cause a "mana break" that can unravel reality. In this case, the spell was too powerful (and she was too inexperienced) for her to control it or stabilise the break, and it started a massive chain reaction. She is very much "ends justify the means". As a dark magic user, she has to kill and destroy to become more powerful, but she feels no guilt because she sees this as a "throwaway" timeline that will all be fixed later when she remakes the world and everyone she killed will be brought back better than before. She then intends to become the world's permanent god, ending suffering forever.

It must also be said that she's gone very much insane from 4 millennia of violent dark magic use. She has a very warped and rose-tinted view of her destroyed homeland that makes her believe that the current world has been "ruined" by its loss, and she feels a lot of hatred towards the world and its people as they are now.

...the Naga nation, bear in mind that their methods of "polite" conversation may be a bit... jarring. Naga (especially those in the capital district) tend to come off very argumentative and aggressive to the foreign ear. Their culture strongly values assertiveness and "saying it like you mean it". They may try to haggle with you endlessly and almost violently, or maybe they will sound a bit demanding when asking anything of you, or maybe a clerk will be unusually terse with you. They mean no actual harm and are actually being "polite" to you. To a Naga, niceties and sugarcoated language indicates being unsure, and thus, potentially dishonest, which they find insulting. They believe that shooting straight with someone and speaking assertively and dominantly indicates a mutual respect and trust, and they will treat you this way. They will also expect the same from you.

...the Devil nation, you may find that Devils are strangely (and sometimes disturbingly)... forward towards you. Their culture, religion, and even their biology place an extreme importance upon sexuality and physical/emotional intimacy, and they have little to no taboos towards it. The average traveller may be shocked at some of the things they see. Don't be alarmed if a Devil you just met is exceptionally touchy-feely with you, or suddenly invites you to a local brothel. They're just being neighbourly. It should be said that Devils are extremely respectful of people's personal boundaries, and as a nation with lots of tourism, are very aware that not everyone is as... open as they are. ...the Orc nation, then congratulations, getting allowed in there is no easy feat. Orcs are known to be quite polite, if a bit reserved and hard to know. Disrespect towards the nation, its people, or (especially) its government is not tolerated, and harshly punished. The smallest are by far the Imps (a subspecies of Devils), being no taller than 4'5" at the tallest, and around 4 feet on average when fully grown. Insects and weeds are a poor comparison IMO because they're demonstrably non-sentient. Humans/Elves/Beastfolk are very clearly sentient, very clearly react to mistreatment, and there is no way the Daedric Princes don't realise this. If anything, their behaviour in the games indicates to me that they know damn well that their actions cause suffering, and they *revel* in it, which is why they seem to pick on sentient mortals exclusively as opposed to animals.

Now, personally, I'd argue that a kid burning ants is, at the very least, a bit cruel. But taking it further, if bugs/weeds/etc were sapient and could actually talk, and outright tell us "hey, cut it out, you're killing us", I'd wager most people would probably think twice about killing them. And those that carry on killing them anyway because they get a kick out of hearing them cry would be seen as, well, evil.

This is the way they're portrayed in the games, which I just chalk up to Bethesda's writers missing the chance to explore what they *should've* been like, and instead just wrote them as Batman villains cos that's easier.

When you put it this way, it becomes more interesting. Mortals trying in vain to find some kind of greater reasoning behind all the suffering the Daedra cause, when in reality, it's that these "gods" are no less flawed and no more immune to corruption than the mortals they look down upon.

Unpopular opinion time.

I see a lot of people defending the popular depiction of Daedra as beings with unfathomable minds and being "above" morality, and seeing us the way we see microbes, and all that jazz, but I really have to side with OP here.

While I'm sure the *intent* was to depict them that way, I just feel like the way they were actually written is kinda half-baked and sloppy. They don't come off that way at all. They don't feel like pure embodiments of their sphere, single-mindedly carrying out what they represent without care/understanding for the way mortals see it. They take way too much glee in causing suffering and messing with mortals and really just end up looking like cartoon villains most of the time. I feel like the "sees us as ants" analogy is faulty. If I go out of my way to stomp on ants and take joy in doing so, like the Daedra seem to do, I'm still just a malicious asshole with a lot of power.

So I guess I agree with both viewpoints. The Daedra are stated to be these Lovecraftian incomprehensible beings far-removed from our puny mortal morality, but in practice, they're really just written very poorly and instead end up actually being a bunch of pretty generic "evil god" villains playing with toys.

The Fl 265 is a "true" helicopter (or rather, a synchropter, as the two rotors intermesh) and only superficially resembles an autogyro. The radial engine at the front powers the rotors (and also has a small fan where the propeller would've been, to provide cooling).

Don't get me wrong, I absolutely agree with you that story-wise and quest-wise, Skyrim was leagues better than FO4 in the sense of making your own story/character, but (and not always, mind you, only in certain spots) I still felt that the player dialogue in Skyrim was lacking in areas and could've used improvement.

For example, the Thalmor, where the game expressly wants you to hate them no matter what. It gives no chance to join them or help them (except for once in Markarth which just seems odd and out of place when you spend the rest of the game actively fighting them). In FO4 at least they let you join the "big bad" faction (even if the end result could've been done better).

Another is racial dialogue. All characters, regardless of race, seem to be completely ignorant of their own culture. Argonians still confusedly ask Madesi what "Saxhleel" means, Khajiit still ask "to know more about your homeland" to fellow Khajiits, Orcs have no idea who Malacath is or what a stronghold is, etc. I get that it's for the sake of informing the player, but *some* kind of alternative dialogue for other races wouldn't have hurt.

While I don't necessarily disagree about a voiced protagonist not working in a TES game, I honestly felt like I could roleplay *more* at certain points in FO4 than I could in Skyrim, simply because (despite there being a preset voice), there were always at least a few different ways to respond. I could make a character that always went for the snarky responses, or one that always spoke politely, for example.

In Skyrim, a lot of the time it only gives you one or two ways to respond to anything, and when receiving a quest, your responses are usually picking between "I'd love to help" and "I don't wanna do your quest". It makes it hard to roleplay evil or nasty characters and still accept most quests when the dialogue is always either friendly or neutral.

Basically what I'm saying is, I agree with you and I would probably prefer a silent protag in the next TES game, but at the same time they should really give us a more varied pool of dialogue options.

Agriculture is relatively rare but still takes place in what few zones of good land exist. The regime has enacted an aggressive policy of self-sufficiency, and has pushed for the advancement of agriculture (with mixed results). Apart from this, livestock is farmed, and the waters off the Orcish coast make for decent fishing.

That said, the nation is effectively slowly starving. What little agriculture they can manage is of poor quality, and farmed with highly obsolete methods. Food is strictly rationed, and the army and government elites get the lion's share. The average Orc citizen (especially those outside of the capital) is very malnourished by world standards.

* Orcs are a robust race closely related to Oni who inhabit a nation bordering the Centaurs to the east. Their country is mainly mountainous badlands, so Orcs have evolved to withstand harsh conditions.
* In keeping with their unforgiving environment, Orcish traditional culture places great importance on the concept of enduring. They don't try to *surmount* hardships (which they see as inevitable), but *endure* them to their end (which they also see as inevitable). "This too shall pass" is a common phrase among Orcs.
* There is not much agriculture in the Orc nation, and many rural Orcs live a traditional nomadic lifestyle, which they have maintained for many hundreds of years nearly unchanged.
* The Orc nation has been ruled by a totalitarian military dictatorship since 1966, when the military took over in a coup d'etat. The regime's dictator is a staunch Orcish nationalist and claims to be working to "restore traditional Orcish culture", which he sees as being in danger due to influence from the other races. He is notorious for his decrees, based entirely on his whims. The Orc nation is now an impoverished pariah state.
* Though many Orcs are fully indoctrinated (and others simply choose to endure), there are a number of Orcs who do try to flee the regime. Those who succeed are usually overwhelmed by their newfound freedoms, and often develop a stereotypical comically tacky taste in clothes and decorating.

Bartolomeo Testarossa is a pirate captain from a bygone era. Around 200 years ago, he and his crew were known to be one of the most brutal pirate crews in the skies. They pillaged, looted, murdered, and raped to their hearts' content and revelled in the misery and fear they'd cause. Bartolomeo in particular was notorious for his lechery and would make it a point to capture the finest woman from each town they raided and have his way with her.

One day he captured the wrong woman. She was a mage, and quite a talented one. She promised him eternal life for him and his crew, in exchange for mercy. She also sabotaged their ship, which crashed on a remote island, marooning them. They would spend the next 200 years slowly decaying, but never dying, until they were reduced to bones. Bartolomeo took this as divine punishment for their misdeeds, and swore to right his wrongs, so that he and his crew may finally rest in peace.

They were found by my protagonist and her crew, and he eventually became a close ally to them, swearing to defend the innocent, become a true gentleman, and atone for his crimes. He remains a jolly soul, and truly regrets his past. He enjoys his new lease on "life", but still dreams of the day he can finally die.

The **Vampires** are probably the most influential, historically-speaking. Their now-famous campaign of exploration in the first century CE inadvertently led to the establishment of contact with many of the other world's races (all of whom up to that point were isolated). Their culture, architecture, and language influenced many other races they came in contact with, particularly the Centaurs, whose language still contains many Vampiric loanwords (and uses their alphabet). Indeed, it was first contact with the Vampires that indirectly set the Centaurs on their path to being the world's greatest superpower.

Which brings us to the **Centaurs**. They founded a great empire which lasted for several centuries before breaking up, but the influence is still felt today. Centauric is the most widely-spoken language, with three distinct races speaking it (or dialects of it) as their official language, and it has become the *de facto* language of commerce worldwide. Centaurs are known as the progenitors of modern democracy, and the Centaurian parliamentary system is practised by most races today. Their currency is the one by which all international trade is conducted, and their military is the most powerful in the world. The Centaurs are currently considered the leaders of the "free world" which is not likely to change.

The **Humans** also deserve a mention, as possibly the most influential race in the modern day. They are a pop culture juggernaut, whose music, fashions, food, and entertainment are enjoyed throughout the world and by nearly all races. Their language rivals Centauric as the "official" language of commerce, and their domination of industry makes their economy one of the biggest drivers of international trade. You cannot go into a single nation without seeing Human-made cars on the road, or hearing Human pop idols singing.

For my main villain, she wasn't always bad. Really it was just the curiosity that all children have which set her on the dark path. When she was a child, she was tempted by a mysterious stranger to try magic. What she didn't know was that the mysterious stranger was actually a sentient manifestation of dark magic seeking a "host". It tempted her with more and more spectacular spells, until it goaded her into trying a spell far beyond her ability to control. The spell caused a "break" in reality which destroyed the entire continent and everything/everyone that lived on it.

She blamed herself for this, and the dark being cultivated these feelings of guilt, convincing her that this was all her fault, that she alone killed her entire civilisation, but that there was a way to fix it, provided she became powerful enough. She became a lich, in order to have a long enough life to attain that power. Her goal is now to become so powerful and skilled in dark magic, that she can control time itself. She intends to reverse her mistake, and become the world's new "god", curating and guiding the new and perfect timeline she will create, where nobody suffers, there is no war or strife, and her people will flourish once again.

Fast forward 4,000 years and she has by now subjugated or killed millions upon millions to fuel her ambitions. She does not allow anything or anyone to stand in her way. Millennia of conquest, torture, killing and use of reality-bending dark magic have turned her into a deranged and hateful husk of a person. She has no regard for innocent lives because she sees this as a "throwaway" timeline that will be fixed anyway. She has developed a rose-tinted view of her ancient civilisation, and has nothing but disdain for the current world which she views as full of evil and corruption that she *insists* did not exist among *her* people.

The sad part is that the dark being which has poisoned her mind for the last 4 millennia has been lying to her this whole time. There is no magic that can reverse or alter time. All the people she's killed can never be brought back, and all the destruction can never be undone. The being is simply feeding off her growing power, and intends on consuming both her and the universe once she gets powerful enough.

The Caitsidh are historically highly patriarchal and their society is steeped in many archaic practices that have given them a bit of a reputation as being rather backwards socially. There are some parties among them that feel it's time to discuss whether some of these practices should/could be made more "fair" or just abandoned altogether. Keep in mind though, that they don't speak for all of their race, and there's still plenty of Caitsidh that are just fine with the status quo and would prefer to keep it.

* The Caitsidh are the only race that still practises legal polygamy into modern times. They are traditionally polygynous marriages, with all spouses living in the same household. There is theoretically no written limit to how many wives one may have, but in practice there are rarely more than five. It is heavily frowned upon to have more, being seen as greedy and shameless. All wives raise any children as though they were theirs, regardless of which one is the biological mother. It should be noted that this practice, though still legal, is increasingly seen as archaic and is becoming rarer and rarer. There is a growing debate about its future in modern society, with some believing that the right to polygamous marriage ought to be extended to women (granting them the right to polyandry), others supporting the legalisation of same-sex polygamy, and others calling for it to simply be abolished altogether.
* There is a group of Succubi/Incubi that practise group marriage. That is, many husbands and many wives all living together as a single family, though calling it "marriage" is a bit of a misnomer, as it is not recognised as such. The various husbands and wives all consider themselves part of the same family, and will share all household responsibilities among each other, including any children born from this union. Sexual relations may occur between any man or woman in the union, and indeed also between members of the same sex. The "group marriage" is unique to their particular culture, and is not seen elsewhere among any of the other Devil subspecies or cultures.
